title: GDPR Basics for Business: Personal Data, Rights and Duties
description: A plain-language course on the EU General Data Protection Regulation for business people who are not data experts. Educational draft: not legal advice, and not yet reviewed by a lawyer.

modules.title: Start here: what the GDPR covers
The rules for using personal data
People's rights: what customers and staff can ask for

concepts.name: Orientation: what the GDPR regulates
concepts.assessment: Name what the GDPR protects and since when it applies.

concepts.name: Supervisory authority
concepts.assessment: Identify the independent public body that monitors the GDPR.

concepts.name: Personal data and the data subject
concepts.assessment: Decide whether information relates to a living natural person.

concepts.name: Identifiable, directly or indirectly
concepts.assessment: Recognise indirect identification through identifiers or combined information.

concepts.name: Pseudonymisation
concepts.assessment: Recognise that pseudonymised data remains personal data.

concepts.name: Anonymous data

concepts.name: Processing

concepts.name: Filing system (paper records)
concepts.assessment: Decide whether manual records are covered.

concepts.name: Controller
concepts.assessment: Identify who determines the purposes and means.

concepts.name: Processor

concepts.name: Joint controllers
concepts.assessment: Recognise joint determination and its consequence for data subjects.

concepts.name: Material scope and the household exemption
concepts.assessment: Decide whether an activity falls outside the GDPR.

concepts.name: Territorial scope
concepts.assessment: Apply the establishment and targeting tests.

concepts.name: Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
concepts.assessment: Spot processing that is hidden or unexpected.

concepts.name: Purpose limitation
concepts.assessment: Check that purposes are specified, explicit and legitimate.

concepts.name: Data minimisation
concepts.assessment: Spot data that is not necessary for the purpose.

concepts.name: Accuracy
concepts.assessment: Choose the right response to inaccurate data.

concepts.name: Storage limitation
concepts.assessment: Decide when identifiable data must no longer be kept.

concepts.name: Integrity and confidentiality
concepts.assessment: Name what appropriate security protects against.

concepts.name: Accountability
concepts.assessment: Identify who must be able to demonstrate compliance.

concepts.name: The six legal bases
concepts.assessment: Match a purpose to a legal basis.

concepts.name: What 'necessary' means
concepts.assessment: Reject a basis when the processing is not necessary for it.

concepts.name: Valid consent
concepts.assessment: Test whether consent is freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous.

concepts.name: Withdrawing consent
concepts.assessment: Apply the withdrawal rules.

concepts.name: Legitimate interests
concepts.assessment: Apply interest, necessity and balancing to a case.

concepts.name: Compatible further processing

concepts.name: Special categories of personal data
concepts.assessment: Recognise Article 9 data.

concepts.name: Conditions for special-category data
concepts.assessment: Recognise that Article 9 is a prohibition with listed exceptions.

concepts.name: Criminal conviction and offence data
concepts.assessment: Recognise the extra condition for criminal data.

concepts.name: Information when collecting from the person
concepts.assessment: Check a privacy notice for its required items.

concepts.name: Information when data comes from elsewhere
concepts.assessment: Apply the timing rules of Article 14.

concepts.name: Response deadline for rights requests
concepts.assessment: Calculate the response deadline and extension rules.

concepts.name: Fees, refusals and identity checks
concepts.assessment: Decide when a fee or refusal is allowed.

concepts.name: Right of access
concepts.assessment: Say what an access response must contain.

concepts.name: Right to rectification
concepts.assessment: Apply rectification and completion.

concepts.name: Right to erasure
concepts.assessment: Find an erasure ground and the exceptions.

concepts.name: Right to restriction
concepts.assessment: Choose restriction for the four listed situations.

concepts.name: Telling recipients about corrections
concepts.assessment: Apply the duty to inform recipients.

concepts.name: Right to data portability
concepts.assessment: Decide whether portability applies.

concepts.name: Right to object
concepts.assessment: Distinguish the general objection from the marketing objection.

concepts.name: Profiling
concepts.assessment: Recognise profiling.

concepts.name: Solely automated decisions
concepts.assessment: Apply Article 22 and its safeguards.

concepts.name: Complaints and court action
concepts.assessment: Choose the route for a data subject.

concepts.name: Compensation and liability
concepts.assessment: Apply the liability rules for controllers and processors.

concepts.name: Appropriate measures and policies
concepts.assessment: Scale measures to risk and demonstrate compliance.

concepts.name: Record of processing activities
concepts.assessment: Draft record entries and test the under-250 exemption.

concepts.name: Data protection by design
concepts.assessment: Choose a design measure that implements a principle.

concepts.name: Data protection by default
concepts.assessment: Choose a compliant default setting.

concepts.name: The controller-processor contract
concepts.assessment: Identify mandatory contract terms.

concepts.name: Sub-processors
concepts.assessment: Apply the authorisation rules for sub-processors.

concepts.name: Security of processing
concepts.assessment: Select risk-appropriate security measures.

concepts.name: Personal data breach
concepts.assessment: Recognise a breach, including loss of availability.

concepts.name: Notifying the supervisory authority
concepts.assessment: Apply the 72-hour rule and its exception.

concepts.name: Telling affected people
concepts.assessment: Decide whether people must be told.

concepts.name: Data protection impact assessment
concepts.assessment: Decide whether a DPIA is required and what it contains.

concepts.name: Data protection officer
concepts.assessment: Decide whether a DPO is mandatory and protect their position.

concepts.name: Integrated compliance review
concepts.assessment: Apply core duties to a fictional business.

concepts.name: International transfer
concepts.assessment: Recognise a transfer to a third country.

concepts.name: Transfer tools
concepts.assessment: Choose adequacy, safeguards or a derogation.

concepts.name: Lead supervisory authority
concepts.assessment: Identify the lead authority for cross-border processing.

concepts.assessment: List what users must be told about cookies.

concepts.assessment: Limit joint control to the operations jointly determined.

concepts.assessment: Explain that AI Act compliance does not settle GDPR questions.

concepts.assessment: Apply the age threshold and parental authorisation.

edges.reason: Identifiability is the test inside the personal-data definition.
Pseudonymised data stays personal data because extra information can still identify the person.
Anonymous data is defined by the absence of identifiability.
Processing is defined as operations performed on personal data.
The filing-system rule decides which manual processing is covered.
A controller is defined as whoever decides the purposes and means of processing.
A processor is defined as acting on behalf of a controller.
Joint controllers are two or more controllers deciding together.
Material scope is stated in terms of automated processing.
Manual processing is covered only through the filing-system rule.
Knowing anonymous data helps explain what falls outside the GDPR.
Article 3 turns on where the controller or processor is established.
Article 3 applies the same tests to processors.
The principles are rules about how processing is carried out.
Purpose limitation governs further processing of collected data.
The controller is the one who sets the purposes.
Necessity is measured against the stated purpose.
Accuracy is judged having regard to the purposes.
The storage period is limited by what the purpose needs.
Anonymising is one way to stop keeping data in identifiable form.
Security protects processing against unauthorised operations and loss.
Accountability places the burden of proof on the controller.
The controller must demonstrate compliance with the principles, so the learner needs them.
Demonstrating compliance covers minimisation, accuracy and storage limits too.
The legal bases are what makes processing lawful under the first principle.
Several bases refer to the controller's obligations, interests or tasks.
Five of the six bases require the processing to be necessary for that basis.
Minimisation uses the same idea of necessity.
Consent is one of the six bases and must be placed among them.
Withdrawal rules apply to consent that was validly given.
The legitimate-interests test includes a necessity step.
Compatibility is the test inside purpose limitation.
Article 6(4) applies when the new purpose is not covered by consent or law.
Special categories are a subset of personal data.
The conditions lift the prohibition on those categories.
Explicit consent builds on the general consent conditions.
Article 9 conditions apply in addition to a legal basis.
Article 10 adds conditions to processing based on Article 6(1).
Criminal data is handled in a similar but separate way.
The notice duties put the transparency principle into practice.
A notice must state the legal basis, so the learner needs the bases.
The controller gives the notice and must identify itself.
A notice must tell people they can complain to the supervisory authority.
Article 14 builds on the Article 13 list and adds items.
The deadlines are duties of the controller.
A refusal must tell the person they can complain to the supervisory authority.
A notice tells people which rights they can request.
Fees and refusals are part of the same Article 12 procedure.
An access request is answered within the Article 12 deadline.
The free first copy and the fee for further copies build on the fee rule.
Rectification is the individual's tool for the accuracy principle.
Rectification requests follow the Article 12 procedure.
One erasure ground is withdrawn consent with no other basis.
One erasure ground is that data is no longer necessary.
Erasure requests follow the Article 12 procedure.
Restriction applies while accuracy is being verified.
Restriction can be chosen instead of erasure of unlawful data.
Article 19 passes erasures on to recipients.
Article 19 also passes restrictions on to recipients.
Portability depends on processing based on consent or contract.
Portability is easier to place next to access.
The general objection targets processing based on legitimate interests or public tasks.
Objections follow the Article 12 procedure.
Profiling is a form of automated processing.
Article 22 covers decisions based on automated processing, including profiling.
One exception is explicit consent, which builds on consent.
A complaint is lodged with a supervisory authority.
Court action is brought against a controller or processor.
Liability rules distinguish the controller's role.
Liability rules limit when a processor is liable.
Compensation claims go to the courts named in Article 79.
Article 24 turns accountability into measures and policies.
The record is one of the measures that demonstrates compliance.
Every record entry states the purposes of processing.
The under-250 exemption does not apply to special categories.
Article 25 is a duty of the controller, decided when it chooses the means.
Design measures implement principles such as minimisation.
Pseudonymisation is the example measure Article 25 names.
Default settings are a specific design obligation.
The contract governs processing by a processor.
Choosing a processor with guarantees is part of the controller's measures.
Sub-processor rules are terms of the processor contract.
Article 32 is a duty of the controller, so the learner needs that role.
Article 32 binds processors as well as controllers.
Article 32 implements the integrity and confidentiality principle.
Pseudonymisation is one of the listed security measures.
A breach is a failure of security.
Notification applies to a personal data breach.
The notification goes to the supervisory authority.
Processors must tell the controller about breaches.
Communication to individuals reuses the notification content.
Encryption that was applied can remove the duty to tell people.
One listed DPIA case is systematic automated evaluation with significant effects.
One listed DPIA case is large-scale special-category data.
A DPIA is a risk-based controller measure.
The DPO is designated by, and advises, the controller or processor.
One mandatory-DPO case is large-scale special-category data.
The DPO cooperates with and is the contact for the supervisory authority.
The DPO advises on DPIAs.
The review starts from the record of processing.
The review checks the processor contracts.
The review includes a breach scenario.
The review decides whether a DPIA is needed.
The review revisits the legal bases.
The review checks the privacy notice.
A transfer is a processing operation.
Scope and transfers are different questions.
The tools are conditions for a transfer.
One derogation is explicit consent to the transfer.
The lead authority is a supervisory authority with a special role.
The lead authority follows the controller's main establishment.
The Board is made up of the supervisory authorities.
Corrective powers belong to supervisory authorities.
A fine is one corrective power, imposed with or instead of the others.
The higher tier names the principles and bases.
The factors set the amount within the tier.
Measures taken under Articles 25 and 32 are a listed factor.
A representative is needed only where Article 3(2) applies.
Schrems II interprets the standard-clauses tool.
Schrems II relies on the power to suspend transfers.
The Framework is an adequacy decision.
The Framework followed the invalidation of Privacy Shield in Schrems II.
Cookie consent uses the GDPR's consent standard.
The information duty is part of the cookie consent rule.
The case refines when and how far joint control applies.
The case requires each joint controller to have a legitimate interest.
The lesson uses Article 22 as the example of a GDPR rule that still applies.
Scope helps place the two laws side by side.
Article 8 adds age conditions to consent.
The orientation lesson explains what law is in force.
